source.excerpt: Baseball always has been and always will be a game demanding team play. You can have the nine greatest individual ball players in the world, but if they don’t play together the club won’t be worth a dime. Two things make for real team play. The first is players’ knowledge of each other that comes from constant playing together. It’s this knowledge which is lacking on all young teams.
trail: The primary is online in full. Project Gutenberg’s transcription ↗ of Babe Ruth’s Own Book of Baseball records the original publication as A. L. Burt Company, 1928.

We searched that text rather than trusting a citation: the sentence occurs exactly once, and the nearest preceding chapter heading is Chapter X. That matches Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗, which also gives a page number, p. 135. Gutenberg’s transcription carries no pagination, so the page is Wikiquote’s figure and not one we could confirm.
Two other Babe Ruth lines in this wave are sourced elsewhere, and we checked: neither “hit or miss big” nor “never gives up” occurs anywhere in this book. This one is genuinely the book’s.
source.excerptNote: The opening of Chapter X, quoted from the Project Gutenberg transcription of the 1928 edition. The chapter goes on to be almost entirely about signs — the mechanics by which nine men stop being nine men.

author.name: Babe Ruth
author.heading: About Babe Ruth
author.bio: George Herman “Babe” Ruth began as a left-handed pitcher for the Boston Red Sox and became, with the New York Yankees, the player who reorganised baseball around the home run. His sixty home runs in 1927 stood as a single-season record for thirty-four years. He put his name to several instructional books in the 1920s, of which the 1928 Own Book of Baseball is the fullest.

context.heading: The individualist arguing against individuals
lead: By 1928 Ruth was the most conspicuously individual athlete alive — he had hit sixty home runs the previous season, more than most entire teams. So there is something bracing about him opening a chapter by insisting that individual greatness is worth nothing on its own, and then spending the rest of it on signs: the small, unglamorous signals by which nine players stop behaving like nine players.

It is also a reminder of what these books were. Ghostwritten or not, they were instructional, aimed at boys and amateur clubs, and the advice is practical rather than inspirational. The line reads today like a motivational poster; in place it is the premise of a lesson about hand signals.
